::: {.callout-note title="Overview"}
This week we focus on three strands of learning:

A.  The linear model with multiple predictors

Last week you learned about regression and the linear model as a way of
predicting one variable from knowledge of one or more other variables.

**This week you will learn about multiple regression which involves the
linear model you learned last week but this time with multiple
predictors i.e., as a way of predicting one variable from knowledge of
more than one variable.**

Regression is really useful when we have more than one predictor which
is why we will be covering multiple regression this week and in week 9.
This week, we will also include a categorical variable (education level)
as a predictor in a linear model.

We will do all this in the context of the **Clearly Understood** project
on how easy or difficult people find it to understand written health
information.

B.  Research project: Building your study on Gorilla

We will also continue the group project by focussing on building your
study on Gorilla, and starting data collection. All relevant materials on this can be found in the Prelab and lab activities sections.

C.  Research project: How to write a report

We will make a start with writing the research report. Relevant materials on this can be found in the lab activities section.

The materials we have prepared to support your learning are arranged in
four parts:

- Lectures
- Reading
- Pre-lab activities
- Lab activities

You can navigate to each in the side bar on the right

## Lectures {#sec-4141-w8-lectures}

::: callout-note
Please note that Rob may mention a different module code or different
week during the lectures. I've reviewed the material and the content is
entirely relevant to the current module.
:::

::: callout-tip
In week 8, we aim to further develop skills in *analysing* and in
*visualising* psychological data. We will do so in the context of the
**Clearly Understood** project.

We will aim to answer the research question: What person attributes in
adult readers predict success in understanding written health
information?

Research questions like this can be examined **using linear models**.

When we do these analyses, we will need to adapt how we report the
results:

- we need to report information about **the model we specify**,
  identifying *all* predictors;
- we will need to decide **if the effects** of one or more predictors
  **are significant**;
- we will report the model **fit statistics** (`F, R-squared`) as well
  as coefficient estimates;
- and we need to learn to write texts **describing the impact** of
  predictors.

Usually, in describing the impacts of predictors, we are required to
communicate:

- the **direction** of the effect -- do values of the outcome variable
  *increase* or *decrease* given increasing values of the predictor?
- the **size** of the effect -- *how much* do values of the outcome
  variable *increase* or *decrease* given increasing values of the
  predictor?

This task of description is enabled by producing plots of the
predictions we can make:

- plots to show we expect the outcome to change, given different values
  of a predictor.
:::

### The lectures have three main areas of focus {#sec-4141-w8-lectures-focus}

**1. Working with the linear model with multiple predictors**

We focus in-depth on how you code linear models, how you identify
critical information in the results summaries, and how you report the
results: the language and the style you can use in your reports.

::: callout-tip
- A small change to `lm()` coding releases tremendous power and
  flexibility in how you use the analysis method.
:::

**2. Analyses are done in context so when we conduct analyses we *must*
use contextual information**

The power and flexibility of the linear model presents challenges. We
must decide *which* predictor variables we specify in our model. This
specification requires us to think about our theoretical assumptions and
what they require us to include to make sense of the behaviours or the
individual differences we observe when we do things like investigating
what makes health information easy or difficult to understand.

**3. Developing critical thinking**

As we develop conceptual understanding and practical skills, we must
learn to *reflect critically* on our analyses, and learn to critically
evaluate the analyses we read about when we read research reports in the
scientific literature.

::: callout-tip
*Critical analysis* can develop by considering

- validity
- measurement
- generalizability
:::

We are always working in the broader context of uncertainty:

- uncertainty about the predictions we may make concerning outcomes of
  interest;
- uncertainty given the possibility that predicted effects may vary
  between individuals or groups;
- uncertainty given the influence of sources of randomness in how
  specific responses are produced.

## Pre-lab activities {#sec-4141-w8-prelab-activities}

After having watched the lectures and read the textbook chapter you'll
be in a good position to try these activities. Completing them before
you attend your lab session will help you to consolidate your learning
and help move through the lab activities more smoothly.

### Pre-lab activity 1: Read the project pre-registration

In the lectures, we discuss how theory should guide which predictor
variables we include in a linear model. A pre-registration is where
researchers set out these choices *before* they collect or analyse their
data.

Read the pre-registered research plan for the **Clearly Understood**
health information research project.

[Read the project pre-registration](https://osf.io/p6fsc/)

As you read, make notes on the following questions:

1.  What is the outcome the researchers want to predict, and how is it
    measured?
2.  Which predictor variables did they plan to include, and what reasons
    do they give for including them?
3.  What did they predict they would find?

::: callout-tip
You already wrote a pre-registration for your own group project. Look at
how this one is set out: it is a useful model for your own in future.
:::

### Pre-lab activity 2: Predict before you look

In the lab, we will fit a linear model that predicts mean accuracy of
understanding (`mean.acc`) from four predictors *at the same time*:

- health literacy (`HLVA`);
- vocabulary knowledge (`SHIPLEY`);
- reading strategy (`FACTOR3`);
- age in years (`AGE`).

Before the lab, write down your predictions:

1.  Which of these four predictors do you expect to have a significant
    effect on `mean.acc` when all four are in the same model?
2.  For each predictor, do you expect the effect to be positive (higher
    scores go with higher accuracy) or negative (higher scores go with
    lower accuracy)?

You can use what you found in the Week 7 lab to help you. Keep your
predictions: you will compare them with the results in Step 5 of the
lab.

## Lab activities {#sec-4141-w8-lab-activities}

### Lab activity 1: What makes it easy or difficult for people to understand written health information?

We will do our practical lab work to develop your skills in the context
of the **Clearly Understood** project.

::: callout-important
The research question we are focussing on today is:

1.  What person attributes predict success in understanding health
    information?
:::

In Week 7, we used linear models with *one* predictor at a time. This
week (Week 8), we extend the linear model in two ways:

1.  We fit linear models with *multiple* predictors. This is why this
    form of analysis is often called *multiple regression*.
2.  We include a categorical (nominal) variable as a predictor, as well
    as numeric variables.

::: {.callout-tip title="Where are the download links?"}
Links to the files to be downloaded are in the **Pre-lab activities
section** under Getting ready.
:::

#### Aims of the activity

We are going to:

1.  Setup the appropriate bits and pieces in RStudio -- using `rm()` and
    `library()`
2.  Read in and inspect the data -- using `read_csv()`, `head()` and
    `summary()`
3.  Recap: draw a histogram and a scatterplot -- using `ggplot()`
4.  Revise: fit a linear model with one predictor, and identify the
    model fit statistics (`F`, `R-squared`) -- using `lm()`
5.  Fit a linear model with multiple predictors -- using `lm()`
6.  Report the results of a linear model with multiple predictors
7.  Plot model predictions -- using `ggpredict()`
8.  Draw boxplots to compare groups -- using `geom_boxplot()`
9.  Fit a linear model with a categorical predictor
10. Extension: Can people accurately evaluate whether they understand
    written health information?

::: callout-tip
Steps 1 to 9 are the main lab activity. If you are short of time, skip
Step 3 (a recap of Week 7) and come back to it later. Step 10 is an
extension: do it if you have time, or after the lab.
:::

#### Step 3: Recap -- draw a histogram and a scatterplot

In Week 7, we did not look at the reading strategy variable `FACTOR3`.
We include it in our model in Step 5, so first take a look at it, using
what you learned in Week 7. If you are short of time, skip this step.

> **Action 1.** Draw a histogram of `FACTOR3`. Set a `binwidth`, use
> `theme_bw()`, edit the labels with `labs()`, set the x-axis limits to
> the possible range of scores (0-80) with `xlim()`, and add a vertical
> line showing the mean.

::: {.callout-tip title="Code" collapse="true"}
``` r
ggplot(data = study.two.gen, aes(x = FACTOR3)) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 2) +
  theme_bw() +
  labs(x = "Reading strategy (FACTOR3)", y = "Frequency count") +
  xlim(0, 80) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = mean(study.two.gen$FACTOR3), colour = "red", linewidth = 1.5)
```

R will show the warning
`Removed 2 rows containing missing values (geom_bar())`. This is not a
problem with the data: `xlim()` removes the two empty bars at the very
edges of the x-axis, which fall just outside the limits.
:::

> **Action 2.** Draw a scatterplot of the association between `FACTOR3`
> (x-axis) and `mean.acc` (y-axis), and edit its appearance as you did
> in Week 7.

::: {.callout-tip title="Code" collapse="true"}
``` r
ggplot(data = study.two.gen, aes(x = FACTOR3, y = mean.acc)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.5, size = 2, colour = "blue", shape = 'square') +
  theme_bw() +
  labs(x = "Reading strategy (FACTOR3)", y = "Mean accuracy") +
  xlim(0, 80) + ylim(0, 1)
```
:::

**Questions Step 3**

a.  What is the direction of the association between `FACTOR3` and
    `mean.acc`? Does it look strong or weak?

#### Step 4: Revise -- fit a linear model with one predictor

We start by revising how to use `lm()` with one predictor: the model of
`mean.acc` and `HLVA` that you fitted in Week 7.

> Action: In a new code chunk, use `lm()` to fit a model with `mean.acc`
> as the outcome and `HLVA` as the predictor. Then get the model
> summary.

::: {.callout-tip title="Code" collapse="true"}
``` r
model.1 <- lm(mean.acc ~ HLVA, data = study.two.gen)
summary(model.1)
```
:::

In Week 7, we looked at the coefficient estimates. This week, we also
look at the information at the bottom of the model summary:

- `Adjusted R-squared` tells us how much of the variation in the outcome
  the model accounts for, as a proportion between 0 and 1.
- `F-statistic` tests whether the model as a whole predicts the outcome
  better than a model with no predictors. It is reported with two
  degrees of freedom (`DF`) and a p-value.

**Questions Step 4**

a.  What is the estimate for the coefficient of `HLVA`, and what does it
    mean in words?
b.  Report the F-statistic (F, the two DF values and the p-value) and
    the Adjusted R-squared.
c.  Explain in words what this R-squared value indicates.

#### Step 5: Fit a linear model with multiple predictors

Now we fit a model that includes **all** of these predictors at the same
time: health literacy (`HLVA`), vocabulary knowledge (`SHIPLEY`),
reading strategy (`FACTOR3`) and age in years (`AGE`). This is the same
model as the one presented in the lectures.

> Action: In a new code chunk, use `lm()` to fit a model with `mean.acc`
> as the outcome and `HLVA`, `SHIPLEY`, `FACTOR3` and `AGE` as the
> predictors. Give the model a new name. Then get the model summary. Try
> to write the code yourself before you look at the Code below.

::: {.callout-note title="How do we add more predictors?"}
We list the predictor variables on the right of the tilde `~`, separated
by a plus sign `+`:

``` r
model <- lm(outcome ~ predictor.1 + predictor.2 + predictor.3, data = data.set)
summary(model)
```

- The model summary now has one row in the `Coefficients` table for each
  predictor.
- Each coefficient estimate shows the predicted change in the outcome
  for a one-unit increase in that predictor, *while holding the other
  predictors constant*.
:::

::: {.callout-tip title="Code" collapse="true"}
``` r
model.2 <- lm(mean.acc ~ HLVA + SHIPLEY + FACTOR3 + AGE, data = study.two.gen)
summary(model.2)
```
:::

**Questions Step 5**

a.  Which predictors have a significant effect on `mean.acc`? Does this
    match the predictions you wrote down in Pre-lab activity 2?
b.  Compare the `HLVA` estimate with the estimate in Step 4. Why do you
    think it has changed?
c.  Compare the Adjusted R-squared with the model in Step 4. What does
    the difference tell you?
d.  Does the `AGE` estimate suggest that older or younger participants
    were more accurate? Is the effect significant?

::: {.callout-note title="Hint" collapse="true"}
- For question b: health literacy and vocabulary knowledge are both
  measures of language experience. How might they be related to each
  other? You can check the correlation between them using
  `correlation()`, as you did in Week 7.
- For question d: think about what a negative estimate means for the
  direction of the prediction line.
:::

#### Step 6: Report the results of a linear model with multiple predictors

When we report a linear model with multiple predictors, we report the
model we specified (the outcome and *all* the predictors), the model fit
statistics (`F` with its degrees of freedom and p-value, and
`Adjusted R-squared`) and, for each predictor, the estimate, `t`, `p`
and the direction of the effect.

> Action: In your Quarto document, write a short report of the model you
> fitted in Step 5. Write it as plain text, not in a code chunk. Use the
> example in the lectures and the template in the Hint.

::: {.callout-note title="Hint" collapse="true"}
Fill in the gaps `...` using the model summary from Step 5.

> We fitted a linear model with mean comprehension accuracy as the
> outcome and health literacy (HLVA), vocabulary knowledge (SHIPLEY),
> reading strategy (FACTOR3) and age (years) as predictors. The model is
> significant overall, F(..., ...) = ..., p ..., and explains ...% of
> variance (adjusted R² = ...). The model estimates showed that the
> accuracy of comprehension increased with higher levels of ... (b =
> ..., t = ..., p ...), ...

- Report the estimate as *b*. In the lecture slides the estimate is
  written as β. In APA style, β is normally used for *standardised*
  estimates, and the estimates from `lm()` are unstandardised, so we use
  *b*. See here for [guidance on APA reporting](https://owl.purdue.edu/owl/research_and_citation/apa6_style/apa_formatting_and_style_guide/apa_tables_and_figures_1.html) 
- Round `t` and `R-squared` to two decimal places. Our estimates are
  small because `mean.acc` runs from 0 to 1, so give *b* to three
  decimal places (e.g. *b* = 0.003, not 0.00).
- Write a leading zero for *b* (e.g. 0.017), but not for p or
  `R-squared` (e.g. p = .005, R² = .36), because these cannot be larger
  than 1.
- When R shows a very small p-value (e.g. `2.87e-12`), report it as
  p \< .001.
:::

#### Step 7: Plot model predictions

In Week 7, we used `geom_abline()` to draw a prediction line from the
intercept and slope of a model with one predictor. With multiple
predictors, the prediction depends on the values of *all* the
predictors, so we use `ggpredict()` from the `{ggeffects}` library. It
works out the predicted outcome across the range of one predictor, while
holding the other predictors constant at their average (mean) values.

> **Action 1.** Use `ggpredict()` to get the predictions for `HLVA` from
> the model you fitted in Step 5. Print the predictions by typing the
> name you gave them, then plot them with `plot()`. Do the same for
> `SHIPLEY`.

::: {.callout-tip title="Code" collapse="true"}
``` r
dat.HLVA <- ggpredict(model.2, "HLVA")
dat.HLVA
plot(dat.HLVA)

dat.SHIPLEY <- ggpredict(model.2, "SHIPLEY")
dat.SHIPLEY
plot(dat.SHIPLEY)
```

- `ggpredict(model.2, "HLVA")` tells R which model to use (`model.2`)
  *and* which predictor we want predictions for (`"HLVA"`, in quotation
  marks).
- The printed predictions show, under `Adjusted for:`, the values the
  other predictors are held at.
- In the plot, the line shows the predicted `mean.acc` and the shaded
  band shows the 95% confidence interval.
- Optional: make prediction plots for `FACTOR3` and `AGE` in the same
  way.
:::

`plot()` zooms the y-axis in on the range of the predictions, so each
plot has a different y-axis. This can make a small effect look large.

> **Action 2.** `plot()` produces a `ggplot`, so you can edit it like
> your other plots. Edit the `HLVA` plot using `theme_bw()`, `labs()`
> and `ylim()`, setting the y-axis to the full possible range of
> `mean.acc` (0-1).

::: {.callout-tip title="Code" collapse="true"}
``` r
plot(dat.HLVA) +
  theme_bw() +
  labs(x = "Health literacy (HLVA)", y = "Predicted mean accuracy", title = "") +
  ylim(0, 1)
```

R will show the message
`Scale for y is already present. Adding another scale for y, which will replace the existing scale.`
This is not an error: it tells you that `ylim()` has replaced the y-axis
that `plot()` set.
:::

**Questions Step 7**

a.  Use the `HLVA` estimate from Step 5 to work out how much predicted
    accuracy changes between an `HLVA` score of 4 and a score of 14.
    Check your answer against the printed predictions.
b.  The estimate for `SHIPLEY` is smaller than the estimate for `HLVA`.
    Does this mean that vocabulary knowledge matters less than health
    literacy? Compare the two prediction plots, and check their axes.

#### Step 8: Draw boxplots to compare groups

Next, we look at a categorical variable: education level (`EDUCATION`).
Participants reported their education as `Further` (further education),
`Higher` (higher education) or `Secondary` (secondary school). A boxplot
shows the distribution of a numeric outcome for each group: the middle
line is the median, and the box holds the middle 50% of scores.

> Action: In a new code chunk, draw boxplots of `mean.acc` for each
> level of `EDUCATION`, with each participant's score shown as a point.

::: {.callout-tip title="Code" collapse="true"}
``` r
ggplot(data = study.two.gen, aes(x = EDUCATION, y = mean.acc)) +
  geom_jitter(width = 0.2, height = 0, alpha = 0.5) +
  geom_boxplot(outlier.shape = NA, colour = "red", alpha = 0.1) +
  theme_bw() +
  labs(x = "Education level", y = "Mean accuracy") +
  ylim(0, 1)
```

- The x variable must be categorical (`EDUCATION`) and the y variable
  numeric (`mean.acc`).
- `geom_jitter()` draws a point for each participant, moved slightly
  left or right so that points do not sit on top of each other.
  `height = 0` keeps each point at the participant's real score.
- `outlier.shape = NA` stops `geom_boxplot()` drawing outlying scores a
  second time, because they are already shown as points.
- See the reference pages for
  [`geom_boxplot()`](https://ggplot2.tidyverse.org/reference/geom_boxplot.html)
  and
  [`geom_jitter()`](https://ggplot2.tidyverse.org/reference/geom_jitter.html).
:::

**Questions Step 8**

a.  Compare the medians of the three groups, and the number of
    participants in each group. Why might the group sizes matter?
b.  Optional: draw the same plot for `ETHNICITY`. What does it show you
    about the participant sample?

#### Step 9: Fit a linear model with a categorical predictor

`lm()` can include categorical variables as predictors, added to the
model in exactly the same way as numeric variables.

> **Action 1.** Fit a model with `mean.acc` as the outcome and `HLVA`,
> `SHIPLEY`, `FACTOR3`, `AGE` *and* `EDUCATION` as predictors. Give the
> model a new name. Then get the model summary.

::: {.callout-tip title="Code" collapse="true"}
``` r
model.3 <- lm(mean.acc ~ HLVA + SHIPLEY + FACTOR3 + AGE + EDUCATION, data = study.two.gen)
summary(model.3)
```
:::

::: {.callout-note title="How does R handle a categorical predictor?"}
- R picks one of the categories (*levels*) to be the *reference*
  (baseline) level. Unless you tell it otherwise, it picks the level
  whose name comes first in the alphabet: here, `Further`.
- The model summary has a row for each of the *other* levels:
  `EDUCATIONHigher` and `EDUCATIONSecondary`.
- Each estimate is the predicted difference in the outcome between that
  level and the reference level, holding the other predictors constant.

There are other ways to code categorical predictors, which you will meet
in later years.
:::

> **Action 2.** Use `ggpredict()` and `plot()` to plot the predicted
> effect of `EDUCATION`.

::: {.callout-tip title="Code" collapse="true"}
``` r
dat.EDUCATION <- ggpredict(model.3, "EDUCATION")
plot(dat.EDUCATION)
```
:::

For a categorical predictor, the plot shows a dot for the predicted
`mean.acc` of each group, and whiskers (lines) showing the 95%
confidence interval: longer lines mean more uncertainty. The 95% refers
to the procedure, not to one particular interval: if we repeated the
study over and over, 95% of the intervals calculated in this way would
contain the true value (Hoekstra et al., 2014).

**Questions Step 9**

a.  Which level of `EDUCATION` is the reference level?
b.  What does the estimate for `EDUCATIONSecondary` mean? Is it
    significant?
c.  In the plot, which group has the longest whiskers? Why do you think
    this is?
d.  Stretch question: in the boxplot in Step 8, the `Secondary` group
    looked noticeably less accurate than the other two groups. Why is
    the difference estimated in the model smaller?

::: callout-tip
You can read more about confidence intervals here:

Hoekstra, R., Morey, R. D., Rouder, J. N., & Wagenmakers, E. J. (2014).
Robust misinterpretation of confidence intervals. *Psychonomic Bulletin
& Review*, 21, 1157-1164.
:::

#### Step 10: Extension -- Can people accurately evaluate whether they understand written health information?

::: callout-important
The second research question in the **Clearly Understood** project is:

2.  Can people accurately evaluate whether they correctly understand
    written health information?
:::

Participants also rated how well they thought they understood each
health text, on a scale from 1 (not at all) to 9 (very well), which gave
us their `mean.self` scores. If people *can* evaluate their own
understanding, their ratings should be associated with their tested
accuracy (`mean.acc`).

> **Action 1.** Fit a model with `mean.self` as the outcome and
> `mean.acc` as the predictor. Then fit a second model the other way
> round: `mean.acc` as the outcome and `mean.self` as the predictor.
> Give each model a different name and get the summaries.

::: {.callout-tip title="Code" collapse="true"}
``` r
model.self <- lm(mean.self ~ mean.acc, data = study.two.gen)
summary(model.self)

model.acc <- lm(mean.acc ~ mean.self, data = study.two.gen)
summary(model.acc)
```
:::

> **Action 2.** Use `ggpredict()` and `plot()` to plot the predictions
> from each model.

::: {.callout-tip title="Code" collapse="true"}
``` r
dat.self <- ggpredict(model.self, "mean.acc")
plot(dat.self)

dat.acc <- ggpredict(model.acc, "mean.self")
plot(dat.acc)
```
:::

**Questions Step 10**

a.  In the model with `mean.self` as the outcome, is `mean.acc` a
    significant predictor? What does this suggest is the answer to
    research question 2?
b.  Compare the two models. Why are the slope estimates so different,
    when the variables and the data are the same? What do you notice
    about the `t` values, p-values and R-squared values?

::: {.callout-note title="Hint" collapse="true"}
- `mean.acc` is scaled from 0 to 1 (the proportion of questions answered
  correctly) and `mean.self` is scaled from 1 to 9 (the average rating).
- A coefficient estimate is the predicted change in the *outcome* for a
  one-unit increase in the *predictor*. What does a one-unit increase
  mean for each of the two variables?
:::

### Lab activity 1:

**Questions Step 2**

a. Which variables are of class `character`?

:::{.callout-note icon=false title="Questions Step 2: Answer" collapse="true"}

a. `participant_ID`, `study`, `GENDER`, `EDUCATION` and `ETHNICITY`. All the other variables are numeric.

:::

**Questions Step 3**

a. What is the direction of the association between `FACTOR3` and `mean.acc`? Does it look strong or weak?

:::{.callout-note icon=false title="Questions Step 3: Answer" collapse="true"}

a. The association is positive: participants with higher reading strategy scores tend to have higher accuracy. There is a lot of scatter around the trend, so the association looks fairly weak. The histogram also shows that all `FACTOR3` scores (29 to 63) sit in the middle of the possible range (0-80).

:::

**Questions Step 4**

a. What is the estimate for the coefficient of `HLVA`, and what does it mean in words?

b. Report the F-statistic (F, the two DF values and the p-value) and the Adjusted R-squared.

c. Explain in words what this R-squared value indicates.

:::{.callout-note icon=false title="Questions Step 4: Answers" collapse="true"}

a. 0.026207. For each one-point increase in health literacy (`HLVA`) score, predicted accuracy increases by 0.026, which is 2.6 percentage points.

b. F-statistic: 56.68 on 1 and 170 DF, p-value: 2.866e-12. In APA style: F(1, 170) = 56.68, p < .001. Adjusted R-squared: 0.2456.

c. The model with `HLVA` as the only predictor accounts for about 25% of the variation in `mean.acc`. About 75% of the variation is not accounted for by this model.

:::

**Questions Step 5**

a. Which predictors have a significant effect on `mean.acc`? Does this match the predictions you wrote down in Pre-lab activity 2?

b. Compare the `HLVA` estimate with the estimate in Step 4. Why do you think it has changed?

c. Compare the Adjusted R-squared with the model in Step 4. What does the difference tell you?

d. Does the `AGE` estimate suggest that older or younger participants were more accurate? Is the effect significant?

:::{.callout-note icon=false title="Questions Step 5: Answers" collapse="true"}

a. Health literacy (`HLVA`), vocabulary knowledge (`SHIPLEY`) and reading strategy (`FACTOR3`) have significant effects (all p < .05). The effect of `AGE` is not significant (p = .055). Whether this matches your predictions will vary.

b. The estimate is 0.017315, smaller than in Step 4 (0.026207), but still positive and significant. In Step 4, `HLVA` was the only predictor. Health literacy and vocabulary knowledge are correlated (r = .39), so in Step 4 part of the `HLVA` estimate reflected the association it shares with vocabulary. In Step 5, each estimate shows the effect of a predictor while holding the others constant, so the `HLVA` estimate now shows the association that is not shared with `SHIPLEY`, `FACTOR3` or `AGE`. The estimate of any one predictor can change depending on which other predictors are in the model. This is one reason why we need to explain why we chose the predictors we include.

c. Adjusted R-squared is 0.3626, compared with 0.2456 in Step 4. The model now accounts for about 36% of the variation in `mean.acc`, compared with about 25%. Adding `SHIPLEY`, `FACTOR3` and `AGE` improves the prediction of `mean.acc`, but about 64% of the variation is still not accounted for.

d. The estimate is -0.001145. It is negative, so predicted accuracy goes down slightly as age goes up: older participants were slightly less accurate, holding the other predictors constant. The effect is not significant (t = -1.935, p = .055), so we should not conclude that there is an age effect in these data. In Week 7, with `AGE` as the only predictor, the estimate was slightly positive (0.0002, p = .76). Older participants in this sample tend to have higher vocabulary scores (r = .29). With `AGE` as the only predictor, part of the vocabulary advantage shows up in the age estimate; once vocabulary is held constant, the remaining age association is slightly negative. The model in the lectures, which used a larger dataset combining both studies, also found a small negative age effect that was not significant.

:::

**Step 6**

:::{.callout-note icon=false title="Step 6: Example report" collapse="true"}

We fitted a linear model with mean comprehension accuracy as the outcome and health literacy (HLVA), vocabulary knowledge (SHIPLEY), reading strategy (FACTOR3) and age (years) as predictors. The model is significant overall, F(4, 167) = 25.32, p < .001, and explains 36% of variance (adjusted R² = .36). The model estimates showed that the accuracy of comprehension increased with higher levels of health literacy (b = .017, t = 4.86, p < .001), vocabulary knowledge (b = .009, t = 4.92, p < .001) and reading strategy (b = .003, t = 2.82, p = .005). Older participants tended to show slightly lower levels of accuracy (b = -.001, t = -1.94, p = .055), but the age effect was not significant.

:::

**Questions Step 7**

a. Use the `HLVA` estimate from Step 5 to work out how much predicted accuracy changes between an `HLVA` score of 4 and a score of 14. Check your answer against the printed predictions.

b. The estimate for `SHIPLEY` is smaller than the estimate for `HLVA`. Does this mean that vocabulary knowledge matters less than health literacy? Compare the two prediction plots, and check their axes.

:::{.callout-note icon=false title="Questions Step 7: Answers" collapse="true"}

a. 10 points × 0.0173 = 0.17. Predicted accuracy increases by about 0.17 (17 percentage points). The printed predictions show 0.67 at HLVA = 4 and 0.85 at HLVA = 14, a difference of 0.18; the small difference from 0.17 comes from rounding.

b. No. A coefficient estimate is the predicted change in the outcome for a one-unit change in the predictor, so its size depends on the scale of the predictor. One point on the `SHIPLEY` scale (0-40) is a smaller step than one point on the `HLVA` scale (1-16). Across the range of scores in this sample, predicted accuracy rises by about 0.16 from the lowest to the highest `SHIPLEY` score (23 to 40) and by about 0.19 from the lowest to the highest `HLVA` score (3 to 14), so the two effects are similar in size. The x-axes of the two plots cover different ranges, and `plot()` zooms each y-axis in on its own predictions, so check the axes before comparing slopes.

:::

**Questions Step 8**

a. Compare the medians of the three groups, and the number of participants in each group. Why might the group sizes matter?

b. Optional: draw the same plot for `ETHNICITY`. What does it show you about the participant sample?

:::{.callout-note icon=false title="Questions Step 8: Answers" collapse="true"}

a. The medians for `Further` (about 0.77) and `Higher` (about 0.79) are similar, and the median for `Secondary` is lower (about 0.68). The groups are very different in size: 98 participants in `Higher`, 59 in `Further` and only 15 in `Secondary`. With so few participants, we can be much less certain about the typical accuracy of the `Secondary` group: a few unusual scores could change its median a lot.

b. Most participants (145 of 172) are `White`, with very few in the `Asian` (15), `Mixed` (7) and `Black` (5) groups. We should be cautious about whether the results of our models apply to people from ethnic minority groups, or to the wider population.

:::

**Questions Step 9**

a. Which level of `EDUCATION` is the reference level?

b. What does the estimate for `EDUCATIONSecondary` mean? Is it significant?

c. In the plot, which group has the longest whiskers? Why do you think this is?

d. Stretch question: in the boxplot in Step 8, the `Secondary` group looked noticeably less accurate than the other two groups. Why is the difference estimated in the model smaller?

:::{.callout-note icon=false title="Questions Step 9: Answers" collapse="true"}

a. `Further` is the reference level, so the summary shows rows for `EDUCATIONHigher` and `EDUCATIONSecondary`.

b. The estimate is -0.044634. Participants with secondary school education are predicted to have `mean.acc` scores about 0.045 (4.5 percentage points) lower than participants with further education, holding health literacy, vocabulary, reading strategy and age constant. The difference is not significant (t = -1.546, p = .124). The difference between `Higher` and `Further` is not significant either (b = 0.001, t = 0.080, p = .936). Adding `EDUCATION` makes almost no difference to how well the model predicts `mean.acc` (adjusted R-squared 0.3658, compared with 0.3626 in Step 5).

c. The `Secondary` group has the longest whiskers. There are only 15 participants in that group, so the prediction for that group is much less certain.

d. In the boxplot, we compared the groups without taking anything else into account. Participants in the `Secondary` group also had lower health literacy and vocabulary scores, on average, than participants in the other groups, and these predict lower accuracy. They were also older, on average. The model estimates the difference between the groups while holding health literacy, vocabulary, reading strategy and age constant, so part of the difference we saw in the boxplot is accounted for by these other predictors.

:::

**Questions Step 10**

a. In the model with `mean.self` as the outcome, is `mean.acc` a significant predictor? What does this suggest is the answer to research question 2?

b. Compare the two models. Why are the slope estimates so different, when the variables and the data are the same? What do you notice about the `t` values, p-values and R-squared values?

:::{.callout-note icon=false title="Questions Step 10: Answers" collapse="true"}

a. Yes. The estimate is 5.5670, t = 8.499, p < .001 (p = 9.36e-15): higher tested accuracy predicts higher self-rated understanding. So people's ratings do reflect their understanding to some extent. But tested accuracy accounts for only about 30% of the variation in self-ratings (adjusted R-squared = 0.2941), so much of the variation in how well people think they understand is not explained by how well they actually understand. People appear able to evaluate their understanding only partly.

b. The slope is 5.5670 in the model with `mean.self` as the outcome and 0.053566 in the model with `mean.acc` as the outcome. A coefficient estimate is the predicted change in the outcome for a one-unit increase in the predictor, so its size depends on the scales of both variables. A one-unit increase in `mean.acc` covers its whole range, from no questions correct (0) to all questions correct (1), and predicts an increase of about 5.6 points on the rating scale. A one-unit increase in `mean.self` is one point on the rating scale, and predicts an increase of about 0.054 in accuracy (5.4 percentage points). The y-axis of each prediction plot uses the scale of that model's outcome. The `t` values, p-values and R-squared values are identical in the two models (t = 8.499, p = 9.36e-15, adjusted R-squared = 0.2941): with one predictor, the strength of the association is the same whichever variable is the outcome. Only the slope changes, because it is expressed in the units of the outcome.

:::
